about.title: How the script works
about.text:
Bengali is written from left to right. There are no capital letters. Most letters hang from a horizontal line along the top called the maatraa; a few letters (such as এ, ঐ, ও, ঙ, ঞ, ৎ) have no top line at all, and several (খ, গ, ণ, থ, ধ, প, শ) have a line with a gap in it - these gaps are part of the letter, not sloppy handwriting.

The script is not an alphabet in the English sense. Each consonant letter stands for a consonant plus a built-in vowel, so ক is not 'k' but 'ko'. To get a different vowel you attach a vowel sign to the consonant: কা kaa, কি ki, কে ke. A vowel has a full, independent letter only when it starts a word or follows another vowel: আম (aam, mango), but নাম (naam, name) with the sign.

A sentence ends with the daanri (।) instead of a full stop. The question mark, comma and exclamation mark are the same as in English.

The traditional order of the letters is scientific: vowels first, then consonants grouped by where in the mouth they are made, from the throat (ক) forward to the lips (ম). Learning them in rows of five makes the sounds much easier to remember.

name (the same vowel as a sign after n)

about.title: The built-in vowel: o, and when it disappears
about.text:
The vowel built into every consonant is written অ when it stands alone. It is NOT the 'a' of Hindi or Sanskrit. It has two pronunciations: an open sound like the 'o' in British English 'hot', and a closed sound like the 'o' in 'go' said short and without gliding. This course writes both as o, because the difference never changes the meaning of the words taught here; copy the audio.

A rough guide: the closed 'o' is used when the next syllable has i or u (অতি oti, মধু modhu), before ক্ষ, জ্ঞ and a য-ফলা (লক্ষ lokkho, সত্য shotto), and at the end of a word. Elsewhere, especially in the first syllable, it is usually the open 'o' (গরম gorom, কলম kolom).

The hard part is knowing when the built-in vowel is silent, because the spelling does not show it.

1. At the end of a word it is usually silent: নাম is naam, not naamo; ফল is phol.

2. It IS pronounced at the end after a conjunct (গল্প golpo, শান্ত shaanto), in many common adjectives and number words (ছোট chhoto, বড় boro, কত koto, এত eto), and in verb endings (করব korbo, করল korlo, করত korto). Modern spelling often writes this final o openly with ো: ভালো bhaalo, এগারো egaaro, করো koro.

3. In the middle of a word it is often dropped to keep the rhythm: আমরা is aamraa, করতে is korte, জানলা is jaanlaa.

The romanisation in this course always shows what is actually said, so when in doubt, trust the roman line.

about.title: Vowel signs
about.text:
Every vowel except অ has two shapes: a full letter, and a sign (called a kaar) that attaches to a consonant. The sign replaces the built-in o.

The signs do not all sit to the right of the consonant. আ-কার ( া ) goes on the right; ই-কার ( ি ) is written on the LEFT although it is spoken after the consonant; ঈ-কার ( ী ) goes on the right; উ, ঊ and ঋ signs hang below; এ-কার ( ে ) and ঐ-কার ( ৈ ) go on the left; ও-কার ( ো ) and ঔ-কার ( ৌ ) wrap around both sides. So কি is ki and কে is ke, even though the sign is written first.

A few consonant + vowel combinations have special shapes you simply have to recognise: গু (gu), রু (ru), রূ (roo), শু (shu), হু (hu), হৃ (hri).

Long and short: ই / ঈ and উ / ঊ were once short and long, but in modern Bengali both members of each pair sound the same. The spelling still matters (it is how you tell কি 'whether' from কী 'what'), and this course keeps it visible by writing i for ই and ee for ঈ, u for উ and oo for ঊ. Do not lengthen ee and oo as you would in English.

examples.english: (yes/no question word) - sign written on the left
the syllable ko - sign on both sides
teacher, guru (special shapes of gu and ru)

about.title: Breathy and plain consonants
about.text:
Bengali consonants come in pairs: a plain one and an aspirated one said with a strong puff of breath - ক k / খ kh, গ g / ঘ gh, চ ch / ছ chh, জ j / ঝ jh, ট t / ঠ th, ড d / ঢ dh, ত t / থ th, দ d / ধ dh, প p / ফ ph, ব b / ভ bh.

The difference changes meaning, so it must be heard and made. English k, t, p at the start of a word are already slightly breathy; the Bengali plain ক, ত, প have NO puff (like the k in 'sky', the t in 'stop', the p in 'spin'), and খ, থ, ফ have much more.

In the romanisation, h after a consonant always means this puff of breath. So th is never the English 'th' of 'think', and ph is not necessarily 'f' (though many speakers do say ফ as f, and ভ close to v). The pair written ch / chh is চ / ছ: ch is like the ch in 'church' without breath, chh the same with breath.

about.title: Two kinds of t and d, and two kinds of r
about.text:
Bengali has two rows of t/d sounds. The dental row - ত থ দ ধ ন - is made with the tip of the tongue touching the back of the upper teeth (like t and d in Spanish or Italian). The retroflex row - ট ঠ ড ঢ ণ - is made with the tongue tip further back, on the ridge behind the teeth, and sounds close to the English t and d. English words borrowed into Bengali are therefore spelt with the retroflex letters: টেবিল (table), ডাক্তার (doctor).

This course does NOT mark the difference in the romanisation: both ত and ট are written t, both দ and ড are d. That keeps the roman line easy to read, but it means you must learn this distinction from the Bengali spelling and the audio. Pairs such as সাত shaat (seven) and ষাট shaat (sixty) differ only in the kind of t.

There are also two r sounds. র is a light tap of the tongue. ড় is a flap: the tongue curls back and flicks forward, a sound between r and d. Both are written r here. ঢ় is the breathy version (written rh) and is rare.

about.title: Nasal sounds
about.text:
The chondrobindu ( ঁ ) written over a letter means that the vowel is spoken through the nose, as in French 'bon'. It is not a separate n sound. This course writes it as an n after the vowel: চাঁদ chaand (moon), পাঁচ paanch (five), হ্যাঁ hyaan (yes). So an n directly after a vowel and before another consonant in the roman line is often only a nasal colouring - check the Bengali spelling.

Nasalisation carries meaning and respect. তার (taar) is 'his/her'; তাঁর (taanr) is the respectful form. বাধা (baadhaa) is 'obstacle'; বাঁধা (baandhaa) is 'tied'.

The sound ng (as in 'sing') is written with ঙ or with the sign ং: রং rong (colour), বাংলা baanglaa. In ঙ্গ a hard g usually follows the ng. The letter ঞ occurs almost only in the conjuncts ঞ্চ (nch) and ঞ্জ (nj), where it is simply an n.

ণ and ন are both pronounced n in modern Bengali.

about.title: Conjuncts and letters you do not pronounce
about.text:
When two consonants come together with no vowel between them, they are written as one combined shape, a conjunct (juktaakkhor). Many are easy to recognise - the first letter is squeezed on top of or beside the second (স্ত = স + ত, ন্ধ = ন + ধ). A few must be learnt as shapes: ক্ষ (ক + ষ), জ্ঞ (জ + ঞ), ঞ্চ, ঙ্গ, ত্র, ক্র, হ্ম.

Several conjuncts are not pronounced the way they are spelt. These are the ones every reader must know.

ক্ষ is kh at the start of a word and kkh in the middle: ক্ষমা khomaa, শিক্ষক shikkhok. There is no s sound in it.

জ্ঞ is g at the start of a word and gg in the middle, and it often turns a following aa into the vowel of 'cat': জ্ঞান gyaan, বিজ্ঞান biggaan.

য-ফলা ( ্য ), the hook written after a consonant: at the start of a word it is silent or changes the vowel to the 'a' of 'cat' (ব্যথা byathaa, ব্যাগ byaag - the y in the roman line stands for that vowel change). In the middle of a word it doubles the consonant before it: অন্য onno, সত্য shotto, ধন্যবাদ dhonnobaad.

ব-ফলা (a small ব under a consonant) is silent at the start of a word and doubles the consonant in the middle: স্বামী shaamee, জ্বর jor, বিশ্বাস bisshaash. (In ম্ব and in ব্ব the b is real: লম্বা lombaa.)

ম-ফলা behaves the same way in many words: স্মৃতি sriti, পদ্ম poddo, আত্মীয় aatteeyo. (But it is a real m after ন, ণ, ল, ম, ঙ, গ and others: জন্ম jonmo.)

The bishorgo ( ঃ ) in the middle of a word doubles the next consonant: দুঃখ dukkho.

র has two special forms: রেফ, a stroke above the following consonant when r comes first (কর্ম kormo), and র-ফলা, a stroke below when r comes second (প্রথম prothom).

about.title: Different letters, same sound
about.text:
Bengali spelling preserves distinctions from Sanskrit that are no longer spoken. For reading you only need to know that these letters sound alike; for writing, the spelling of each word has to be learnt.

শ, ষ and স are all pronounced sh in native words: শাক shaak, ষাট shaat, সাত shaat. They become a true s only in certain conjuncts - before ত, থ, ন, র, ল (রাস্তা raastaa, স্নান snaan, শ্রী sree, প্রশ্ন prosno) - and in many English loanwords (বাস baas 'bus', সাইজ saaij 'size'). The romanisation shows which is said.

জ and য are both j: জল jol, যাই jaai. The letter য় (with a dot) is different: it is a y-glide between vowels or at the end of a word (সময় shomoy, মেয়ে meye). After ও it sounds like a w, so ওয়া is written owaa: খাওয়া khaaowaa.

ন and ণ are both n. ই / ঈ are both i; উ / ঊ are both u (written i / ee and u / oo here only to mirror the spelling). ত and ৎ are the same t; ৎ is the form used when no vowel follows. ঙ and ং are the same ng.

The vowel এ has two sounds: usually the e of 'bed', but in many common words the a of 'cat' - এক (one), কেন (why), কেমন (how), দেখা (to see), এখন (now), খেলা (to play). The same 'cat' vowel is spelt অ্যা at the start of loanwords (অ্যাম্বুলেন্স). This course writes এ as e in both cases and tells you in a note when it is the 'cat' sound.

I go (the letter y, said j)

about.title: The romanisation used in this course
about.text:
The roman line shows how a phrase is pronounced, not how it is spelt letter by letter. It is always in lower case.

Vowels: o = অ (built-in vowel) and ও; aa = আ, the a of 'father'; i = ই and ee = ঈ, both the i of 'machine' said short; u = উ and oo = ঊ, both the u of 'put'; e = এ (see the note on its two sounds); oi = ঐ; ou = ঔ; ri = ঋ. A single a (in ya, yaa, or at the start of a loanword) is the a of 'cat': byaag, hyaan, ambulens. When two vowels stand together, say both: khaai = khaa-i, jaao = jaa-o, dii = di-i.

Consonants: k kh g gh ng; ch chh j jh; t th d dh n (for both the dental and the retroflex rows); p ph b bh m; r (র and ড়), rh (ঢ়), l; sh (শ ষ স), s where a true s is said; h; j also for য; y for য়; w for the glide in ওয়া.

h after a consonant = a puff of breath (kh, gh, chh, jh, th, dh, ph, bh). The one exception is sh.

n after a vowel can be the nasal sign: paanch, hyaan, taanr.

A doubled consonant is held longer: onno, dukkho, bisshaash. The cluster চ্ছ is written chchh (aachchhaa), since chh is already one sound.

The two forms নও ('you are not') and হও ('you become') are written nou and hou; say no-o and ho-o.

The built-in vowel is written only where it is said: naam, gorom, golpo.

about.title: Kolkata and Dhaka
about.text:
This course teaches the standard colloquial language (cholito bhaashaa) as spoken in Kolkata and West Bengal. It is understood everywhere Bengali is spoken, including Bangladesh, and the grammar and almost all of the vocabulary are shared.

The differences you will notice first are a handful of everyday words. West Bengal says জল (jol) for water, Bangladesh says পানি (paani). Other pairs: নুন / লবণ (salt), স্নান / গোসল (bath), মাংস / গোশত (meat), জলখাবার / নাস্তা (breakfast, snack), নমস্কার / আসসালামু আলাইকুম (greeting), দাদা / ভাই or ভাইয়া (elder brother), দিদি / আপা (elder sister), সঙ্গে / সাথে (with), নেমন্তন্ন / দাওয়াত (invitation). Many of these follow religion as much as geography.

Some verb forms differ slightly: Kolkata prefers the shortened forms taught here (গেছি gechhi, ঘুমোচ্ছে ghumochchhe, তিনটে tinte), where Bangladesh standard prefers the fuller ones (গিয়েছি, ঘুমাচ্ছে, তিনটা).

The unit notes point out the variants that matter. Whichever you use, you will be understood on both sides of the border.

units.title: Greetings & basics
units.description: Say hello and goodbye, ask how someone is, thank people and give simple answers.

guide.title: Hello and goodbye
guide.text:
Bengali has no everyday 'good morning' or 'good afternoon'. One greeting serves all day, and the same word is used when you leave.

নমস্কার (nomoshkaar) is the usual greeting in West Bengal and among Hindus, often said with the palms together. Muslims, and most people in Bangladesh, greet with আসসালামু আলাইকুম (aassaalaamu aalaaikum); the reply is ওয়ালাইকুম আসসালাম. With friends, people skip the greeting altogether and go straight to 'how are you?'.

শুভ রাত্রি (good night) and শুভ সকাল (good morning) exist, but they are translations of the English phrases: you will see them in messages and hear them on television more than in the street.

When leaving, a Bengali does not say 'I am going' - that sounds unlucky. You say আসি (aashi), literally 'I come', meaning 'I'll be back'.

guide.title: How are you?
guide.text:
The question is 'you how are?': আপনি কেমন আছেন? The verb comes last, as it always does in Bengali. The answer simply swaps in 'I' and changes the verb ending: আমি ভালো আছি, 'I well am'.

Notice the two endings: আছেন (aachhen) goes with আপনি, the polite 'you'; আছি (aachhi) goes with আমি, 'I'. Bengali verbs change with the person and with the level of respect, but never for gender or for singular and plural.

Bengali has three words for 'you'. This course uses the polite আপনি (aapni) until the unit on pronouns; it is the right choice for any adult you do not know well. To a friend you would say তুমি কেমন আছ? (tumi kemon aachho).

The e in কেমন is the open sound of the a in 'cat'.

guide.title: Thank you, sorry, okay
guide.text:
ধন্যবাদ (dhonnobaad) means 'thank you', but it is more formal than the English word and used far less: between friends and family, thanks are shown with a smile or a nod, and saying ধন্যবাদ for every small thing sounds distant. Use it freely with strangers, in shops and in offices. Spelling trap: the ন্য is said as a long n - dhon-no-baad.

মাফ করবেন (maaph korben) is literally 'you will forgive': it covers both 'sorry' and 'excuse me'.

ঠিক আছে (thik aachhe), 'it is right', is the universal 'okay', 'fine', 'all right'.

হ্যাঁ (hyaan) is 'yes' and না (naa) is 'no'. The vowel of হ্যাঁ is the a of 'cat', said through the nose.

The everyday greeting among Muslims and throughout Bangladesh. Reply: ওয়ালাইকুম আসসালাম (owaalaaikum aassaalaam).

In conversation the আমি is usually dropped: ভালো আছি।
The written ন্য is pronounced as a doubled 'nn'. More formal than English 'thanks'.
The vowel is like the 'a' in English 'cat', nasalised.
The same word placed after a verb means 'not'.
How a guest is welcomed. The ending -un is the polite command.
The polite way to take your leave: you say 'I come', never 'I go'.
Rather formal; modelled on the English phrase.

units.title: Introductions
units.description: Introduce yourself, say where you are from and what you do, and ask the other person the same.

guide.title: My name is ...
guide.text:
Bengali has no word for 'is' in sentences that say what something is. 'My name is Raj' is simply 'my name Raj': আমার নাম রাজ। 'I am a student' is 'I student': আমি ছাত্র।

There is also no word for 'a' or 'the' here. You just put the two things side by side.

আমার (aamaar) is 'my' and আপনার (aapnaar) is the polite 'your'. They come before the noun, as in English.

The question word stays where the answer will go, so 'What is your name?' is 'your name what?': আপনার নাম কী? Note the spelling কী with the long vowel sign: that is the word 'what'. (The short-vowel কি is a different word, met in the unit on questions.)

guide.title: Where are you from?
guide.text:
Words like 'from', 'in', 'with' come AFTER the noun in Bengali, so they are called postpositions. থেকে (theke) is 'from': আমেরিকা থেকে, 'America from'.

'Where are you from?' is asked as 'where have you come from?': আপনি কোথা থেকে এসেছেন? The answer uses the same verb with the 'I' ending: এসেছি (eshechhi).

Between Bengalis the usual question is আপনার বাড়ি কোথায়? - 'where is your home?' - which asks about your home town or ancestral place rather than your present address.

'In' a place is shown by an ending on the place name: কলকাতা becomes কলকাতায় (kolkaataay), 'in Kolkata'. The unit on case endings explains the rule.

guide.title: Introducing someone else
guide.text:
Bengali has no 'he' and 'she': one word covers both. But it does distinguish respect. For someone standing next to you whom you introduce politely, use ইনি (ini), 'this person (respected)'. For someone further away, উনি (uni), 'that person (respected)'.

Again there is no 'is': ইনি আমার বন্ধু, 'this-person my friend'.

When you have been introduced, the set phrase is আপনার সঙ্গে আলাপ হয়ে ভালো লাগল - literally 'having become acquainted with you, it felt good'. সঙ্গে (shonge) is the postposition 'with'; in Bangladesh you will more often hear সাথে (shaathe).

units.title: Yes, no and polite words
units.description: Answer yes and no naturally, ask politely without a word for 'please', and address strangers the Bengali way.

guide.title: Yes and no
guide.text:
হ্যাঁ (hyaan) is yes and না (naa) is no. But a bare yes or no can sound abrupt. The natural answer repeats the verb of the question: 'Is there tea?' - 'There is' (আছে), or 'There isn't' (নেই).

নেই (nei) is a word to learn at once. It means 'there is not', 'is not here', 'do not have', and it never changes its form.

আচ্ছা (aachchhaa) is the all-purpose 'all right', 'I see', 'okay then'. You will hear it constantly. A polite, slightly old-fashioned 'yes' to an elder or a customer is আজ্ঞে (aagge).

guide.title: There is no everyday word for 'please'
guide.text:
Politeness in Bengali is built into the verb. The polite command ends in -un: বসুন (boshun) is already 'please sit'. Using আপনি and the -un form is all the politeness a normal request needs.

To soften a request further, add একটু (ektu), 'a little': একটু শুনুন, 'listen a little', has the feel of 'could you listen for a moment?'.

An even gentler request uses the future tense as a question: একটু শুনবেন? - 'will you listen a little?'

দয়া করে (doyaa kore), literally 'doing kindness', is the dictionary translation of 'please'. It is correct but formal: you see it on signs and hear it in announcements, and it is fine when you are asking a real favour.

examples.english: Excuse me, could you listen a moment?

guide.title: How to address people
guide.text:
Strangers are addressed with family words, chosen by their age relative to yours. In West Bengal a man of about your age or older is দাদা (daadaa, elder brother) and a woman is দিদি (didi, elder sister). An older man is কাকু (kaaku, uncle) and an older woman মাসিমা (maashimaa, aunt). In Bangladesh the usual words are ভাই (bhaai) and আপা (aapaa), with চাচা (chaachaa) and খালা (khaalaa) for older people.

These words are also added after a first name as a mark of respect: রাজদা, মিতাদি (short for দাদা and দিদি).

To get someone's attention, start with the address word: দাদা, একটু শুনুন।

Replying to thanks, people say ও কিছু না, 'that is nothing'.

guide.title: Saying sorry
guide.text:
মাফ করবেন (maaph korben), 'you will forgive', is the everyday apology and also 'excuse me'. ক্ষমা করবেন (khomaa korben) means the same and is a little more formal.

কিছু মনে করবেন না (kichhu mone korben naa), 'do not take anything to mind', is 'please don't mind', said before or after doing something that might offend.

আমি দুঃখিত (aami dukkhito) is 'I am sorry' in the sense of 'I regret'; it is formal and is not used for bumping into someone. The ঃ doubles the kh: duk-khi-to.

units.title: Numbers 1-10
units.description: Count from zero to ten, read the Bengali digits and ask for one or two of something.

guide.title: The digits
guide.text:
Bengali has its own digits: ০ ১ ২ ৩ ৪ ৫ ৬ ৭ ৮ ৯. They are used on price tags, bus numbers, calendars and banknotes, side by side with the international digits, and they are combined in exactly the same way: ১০ is 10, ২৫ is 25, ১০০ is 100.

Two of them mislead English readers: ৪ (four) looks like an 8, and ৭ (seven) looks like a 9. ৫ (five) and ৬ (six) also need a second look.

Pronunciation notes: the এ of এক (one) is the a of 'cat'. পাঁচ (five) has a nasal vowel, not a real n. সাত (seven) is written with স but said shaat. ছয় (six) and নয় (nine) end in the y-glide.

guide.title: Counting things: add -taa
guide.text:
In Bengali you rarely put a bare number in front of a noun. When you count things, the number takes a small ending called a classifier. The everyday one is -টা (-taa): একটা (ektaa) 'one (of something)', পাঁচটা (paanchtaa) 'five'.

Three of the forms are irregular in Kolkata speech and must be learnt: দুটো (duto) 'two', তিনটে (tinte) 'three', চারটে (chaarte) 'four'. From five onwards it is always -টা. (In Bangladesh you will hear দুইটা, তিনটা, চারটা.) Before the classifier, ছয় and নয় shorten: ছটা (chhotaa), নটা (notaa).

The noun itself does not change for the plural: দুটো চা, 'two tea'.

For people the classifier is -জন (-jon): একজন, দুজন, তিনজন.

The bare number is used when counting aloud, in arithmetic, and before measure words: এক কাপ চা, 'one cup of tea'.

units.title: Reading: spelling versus sound
units.description: Read aloud words whose pronunciation differs from their spelling: silent letters, doubled consonants and the hidden vowel.

guide.title: Is the last vowel said?
guide.text:
Every consonant carries a built-in o, but at the end of a word it is usually dropped: নাম is naam, ফল is phol, সময় is shomoy.

It is kept in three situations you will meet all the time.

After a conjunct: গল্প golpo, শান্ত shaanto, বন্ধ bondho (closed).

In a set of very common adjectives and quantity words: ছোট chhoto (small), বড় boro (big), কত koto (how much), এত eto (so much), ভালো bhaalo (good - nowadays spelt with the vowel sign).

In verb endings: করব korbo (I will do), করল korlo (he did), করত korto (he used to do).

There is no rule that settles every case, so learn each new word with its sound.

guide.title: The silent hooks: ব-ফলা, ম-ফলা, য-ফলা
guide.text:
Three consonants, when attached below or beside another consonant, are usually not pronounced as themselves.

A small ব under a letter is silent at the start of a word: স্বাগত is shaagoto, জ্বর is jor. In the middle of a word it lengthens the consonant it hangs from: বিশ্বাস is bisshaash.

A small ম often does the same: পদ্মা is poddaa, আত্মীয় is aatteeyo, লক্ষ্মী is lokkhee.

The hook ্য (য-ফলা) lengthens the consonant in the middle of a word: সত্যি is shotti, অন্য is onno, ধন্যবাদ is dhonnobaad. At the start of a word it is not a consonant at all - it turns the vowel into the a of 'cat': ব্যথা byathaa, ব্যাগ byaag. After a conjunct it is silent: সন্ধ্যা is shondhaa.

The sign ঃ inside a word also lengthens the next consonant: দুঃখ is dukkho.

guide.title: ক্ষ and জ্ঞ
guide.text:
ক্ষ is written ক + ষ but has no s or sh sound. At the start of a word it is kh: ক্ষমা khomaa (forgiveness). In the middle it is a long kkh: শিক্ষক shikkhok (teacher), লক্ষ্মী lokkhee.

জ্ঞ is written জ + ঞ but is pronounced g. At the start of a word it is g, and a following আ becomes the a of 'cat': জ্ঞান is gyaan (knowledge). In the middle it is a long gg: বিজ্ঞান biggaan (science).

guide.title: sh or s? e or 'cat'?
guide.text:
শ, ষ and স are all sh in ordinary words: শাক shaak, ষাট shaat, সাপ shaap. A true s is heard when one of them is joined to ত, থ, ন, র or ল - রাস্তা raastaa, স্নান snaan, শ্রাবণ sraabon - and in many English loanwords: বাস baas, সিট sit.

The vowel এ is the e of 'bed' in most words (দেশ desh, মেয়ে meye) but the a of 'cat' in a number of very common ones: এক ek (one), কেন keno (why), কেমন kemon (how), দেখা dekhaa (to see), এখন ekhon (now), এত eto (so much). The spelling gives no sign of this. The notes in this course point it out; listen to the audio and imitate.

phrases.note: The ব under স is silent. Seen on signs and heard in speeches; at home people say আসুন, আসুন.

The ব under শ is not a b: it lengthens the sh.

ত্য is a long t.

Both words keep their final o: after a conjunct in গল্প, and by habit in ছোট.
After a conjunct the য-ফলা is silent. The everyday Kolkata word is সন্ধে (shondhe).
The e is the a of 'cat', and the final o is said.

ঠ and ড are retroflex: the tongue tip is behind the gum ridge, not on the teeth. In Bangladesh: পানি (paani).

units.title: Word order and 'to be'
units.description: Build simple sentences with the verb at the end, and know when Bengali needs a word for 'is' and when it does not.

guide.title: The verb comes last
guide.text:
The basic order of a Bengali sentence is subject - object - verb. English says 'I eat rice'; Bengali says 'I rice eat': আমি ভাত খাই।

Everything else - time, place, manner - goes between the subject and the verb, usually in the order time, then place: 'I today at-home rice will-eat'.

Because the verb ending already shows who is acting, the subject pronoun is often left out when it is obvious: ভাত খাই can mean 'I eat rice' on its own.

The order of the other words is fairly free and is used for emphasis, but while you are learning, keep the verb at the end and you will always be right.

guide.title: No word for 'is' when you say what something is
guide.text:
When a sentence says that A is B - a name, a profession, a description - present-tense Bengali uses no verb at all. The two parts are simply placed together.

এটা আমার বই - 'this my book' - This is my book.
উনি ডাক্তার - 'that-person doctor' - He/She is a doctor.
চা খুব গরম - 'tea very hot' - The tea is very hot.

This 'zero verb' only exists in the present. For the past you need ছিল (chhilo, 'was'), and the negative has its own word, নয় (noy, 'is not'); both are taught in later units.

guide.title: আছে: 'is' for where things are and what exists
guide.text:
When 'is' means 'is located' or 'there is', Bengali uses the verb আছে (aachhe).

বইটা টেবিলে আছে - The book is on the table.
এখানে একটা দোকান আছে - There is a shop here.

আছে takes the usual endings: আমি আছি (I am), তুমি আছ (you are, familiar), সে আছে (he/she/it is), আপনি আছেন (you are, polite), তিনি আছেন (he/she is, respected). That is why 'mother is at home' has আছেন: mothers are spoken of respectfully.

Compare: উনি ডাক্তার (He is a doctor - what he is: no verb) and উনি বাড়িতে আছেন (He is at home - where he is: আছেন).

The same verb gives 'how are you?': আপনি কেমন আছেন? - a temporary state, so আছেন is used.

examples.english: The book is on the table.

guide.title: No 'a', no 'the', no gender
guide.text:
Bengali has no articles and no grammatical gender. বই can be 'a book', 'the book' or 'books'; the context decides.

When you need to be specific, there are two tools. The ending -টা (-taa) on a noun makes it definite, like 'the': বইটা, 'the book'; ঘরটা, 'the room'. And একটা (ektaa, 'one') before a noun works like 'a': একটা বই, 'a book'.

Nouns do not change in the plural after a number or when the meaning is general, and adjectives never change at all: বড় ঘর is 'big room' or 'big rooms'.

phrases.note: ভাত is cooked rice; uncooked rice is চাল (chaal).

units.title: Pronouns and respect
units.description: Choose the right word for 'you' and 'he/she' - polite, familiar or intimate - and match the verb ending to it.

guide.title: Three words for 'you'
guide.text:
Bengali makes you choose a level of respect every time you say 'you'.

আপনি (aapni) - polite. For strangers, older people, teachers, officials, your friends' parents, anyone you would call Mr or Ms. When in doubt, use this.

তুমি (tumi) - familiar. For friends, colleagues of your own age, your spouse, children, and usually your own parents and relatives. Moving from আপনি to তুমি is a step of friendship, and the older or senior person normally suggests it.

তুই (tui) - intimate. For close childhood friends, younger brothers and sisters, small children, and by some people to servants or in anger. Used to the wrong person it is insulting. Learn to recognise it; do not use it until a Bengali friend uses it with you.

The plurals are আপনারা (aapnaaraa), তোমরা (tomraa) and তোরা (toraa).

guide.title: The verb ending follows the pronoun
guide.text:
Each level has its own verb ending, and the same five endings run through every tense. In the simple present of করা (to do) they are:

আমি করি - I do (-i)
তুমি করো - you do, familiar (-o)
তুই করিস - you do, intimate (-ish)
সে করে - he/she does, ordinary (-e)
আপনি করেন, তিনি করেন - you do (polite), he/she does (respected) (-en)

Notice that polite 'you' and respected 'he/she' share one ending. The verb is the same for singular and plural: আমরা করি 'we do', তারা করে 'they do'.

Because the ending tells you the level, mixing them - আপনি with a তুমি ending - is a real mistake, like saying 'you is' in English, and it can sound rude.

guide.title: He and she: one word, two levels, three distances
guide.text:
There is no difference between 'he' and 'she'. Instead Bengali marks respect and distance.

Ordinary (for friends, children, people you would call তুমি or তুই, and in neutral narration): সে (she) 'he/she' in general; ও (o) 'he/she over there'; এ (e) 'he/she right here'.

Respected (for anyone you would call আপনি, and for elders): তিনি (tini); উনি (uni) 'that person there'; ইনি (ini) 'this person here'. These take the -en ending.

In everyday speech ও and উনি are the commonest; সে and তিনি are used for someone not present and in writing.

Plurals: তারা (taaraa), ওরা (oraa), এরা (eraa) 'they'; respected তাঁরা (taanraa), ওঁরা (onraa), এঁরা (enraa) - spelt with the nasal sign. 'It' for a thing is সেটা, ওটা or এটা.

guide.title: The full set
guide.text:
I: আমি (aami) - we: আমরা (aamraa)
you, polite: আপনি - আপনারা
you, familiar: তুমি - তোমরা
you, intimate: তুই - তোরা
he/she, ordinary: সে, ও, এ - তারা, ওরা, এরা
he/she, respected: তিনি, উনি, ইনি - তাঁরা, ওঁরা, এঁরা

As the object of a verb ('me', 'you', 'him/her') the pronouns take the ending -কে: আমাকে (aamaake), আপনাকে (aapnaake), তোমাকে (tomaake), তোকে (toke), তাকে (taake), ওকে (oke), তাঁকে (taanke), ওঁকে (onke). The possessive forms ('my', 'your') are in the next unit.

units.title: My, your, his: the ending -r
units.description: Say whose something is, using the possessive forms of the pronouns and the ending -r / -er on nouns.

guide.title: My, your, his, her, our, their
guide.text:
The possessive pronouns all end in -r. They go before the noun and never change, whatever is owned.

আমার (aamaar) my - আমাদের (aamaader) our
আপনার (aapnaar) your, polite - আপনাদের (aapnaader)
তোমার (tomaar) your, familiar - তোমাদের (tomaader)
তোর (tor) your, intimate - তোদের (toder)
তার (taar), ওর (or), এর (er) his/her, ordinary - তাদের, ওদের, এদের their
তাঁর (taanr), ওঁর (onr), এঁর (enr) his/her, respected - তাঁদের, ওঁদের, এঁদের

The same level of respect applies as with the subject pronouns: use আপনার to someone you call আপনি, and তাঁর or ওঁর about someone you would call আপনি.

Used alone they mean 'mine', 'yours': এটা আমার, 'this is mine'. কার (kaar) is 'whose'.

guide.title: -r and -er on nouns
guide.text:
Any noun or name becomes possessive with the same ending, like the English 's.

After a vowel, add -র (-r): বাবা - বাবার (baabaar) father's; বাড়ি - বাড়ির (baarir) of the house; বন্ধু - বন্ধুর (bondhur) friend's.

After a consonant, add -এর (-er): রাজ - রাজের (raajer) Raj's; দোকান - দোকানের (dokaaner) of the shop.

A few short words ending in a vowel take -য়ের (-yer): মা - মায়ের (maayer) mother's; চা - চায়ের (chaayer) of tea; ভাই - ভাইয়ের (bhaaiyer) brother's; বই - বইয়ের (boiyer) of the book.

With the definite ending -টা the possessive is -টার: বইটার (boitaar), 'of the book'.

guide.title: The same ending means 'of'
guide.text:
Bengali uses the possessive wherever English uses 'of', and often where English just puts two nouns together. The owner or the describing word comes first.

বাড়ির চাবি - 'house's key' - the house key
চায়ের দোকান - 'tea's shop' - a tea shop
কলকাতার রাস্তা - 'Kolkata's roads' - the streets of Kolkata
খবরের কাগজ - 'news's paper' - newspaper

Most postpositions also need this ending on the word before them: আমার সঙ্গে 'with me', টেবিলের উপরে 'on the table', আপনার জন্য 'for you'. You will meet them in the next unit.

নিজের (nijer) is 'own': আমার নিজের বাড়ি, 'my own house'.

phrases.note: To a child or someone of your own age in an informal setting.
-er after a consonant.
মা takes -yer.
-r after a vowel.
Numbers are asked with কত (how much), not কী (what).
তাঁর, with the nasal sign, is the respectful form; the ordinary form is তার (taar).

units.title: To, in, from, with: case endings
units.description: Mark who receives an action and where things happen, with the endings -ke and -e / -te and the postpositions theke, diye, shonge, jonno.

guide.title: -ke: the person on the receiving end
guide.text:
The ending -কে (-ke) marks the person an action is directed at. It covers both the English direct object ('I know Raj') and 'to' ('give it to Raj').

আমি রাজকে চিনি - I know Raj.
রাজকে বলুন - Tell Raj.

It is used for people and animals, and for things only when they are specific and you want to single them out. Ordinary things as objects take no ending at all: আমি ভাত খাই, 'I eat rice'; আমি বইটা পড়েছি, 'I have read the book'.

When a sentence has both a person and a thing, the person gets -কে and comes first: আমাকে একটা কলম দিন, 'me-to a pen give'.

The pronoun forms: আমাকে, আপনাকে, তোমাকে, তোকে, তাকে, ওকে, তাঁকে, ওঁকে; plural আমাদের, আপনাদের, তোমাদের, তাদের, ওদের (the plural object forms are the same as the possessive).

guide.title: -e, -te, -y: in, at, on, to
guide.text:
One ending does the work of 'in', 'at', 'on' and, with verbs of movement, 'to'. Its shape depends on the last sound of the word.

After a consonant: -এ (-e). ঘর - ঘরে (ghore) in the room; বাজার - বাজারে (baajaare) at/to the market; টেবিল - টেবিলে (tebile) on the table.

After আ (aa): -য় (-y). কলকাতা - কলকাতায় (kolkaataay); ঢাকা - ঢাকায় (dhaakaay); রাস্তা - রাস্তায় (raastaay) on the road. (-তে is also heard: ঢাকাতে.)

After any other vowel: -তে (-te). বাড়ি - বাড়িতে (baarite) at home; দিল্লি - দিল্লিতে (dillite) in Delhi.

With a verb of going, the ending is often left off a destination: আমি বাড়ি যাচ্ছি, 'I am going home'; আমি কলকাতা যাব, 'I will go to Kolkata'.

The same ending also means 'by' a means of transport: বাসে (baase) by bus, ট্রেনে (trene) by train, ট্যাক্সিতে (tyaaksite) by taxi.

examples.english: I am going to the market.

guide.title: Postpositions: from, with, for
guide.text:
Other relationships are shown by separate words placed after the noun.

থেকে (theke) 'from, since' follows the plain noun: দিল্লি থেকে, 'from Delhi'; কাল থেকে, 'since yesterday'.

দিয়ে (diye) 'with (a tool), by way of' also follows the plain noun: হাত দিয়ে, 'with the hand'; ছুরি দিয়ে, 'with a knife'; এই রাস্তা দিয়ে, 'along this road'.

সঙ্গে (shonge) 'with, together with' needs the possessive -r on the word before it: বন্ধুর সঙ্গে, 'with a friend'; আমার সঙ্গে, 'with me'. Bangladesh usage prefers সাথে (shaathe).

জন্য (jonno) 'for' also needs the possessive: আপনার জন্য, 'for you'; বাবার জন্য, 'for father'. (জন্যে is a common spoken variant.)

কাছে (kaachhe) 'near; to or at a person' takes the possessive too: স্টেশনের কাছে, 'near the station'; ডাক্তারের কাছে, 'to the doctor'.

examples.english: I am going with a friend.
The shop is near the station.

guide.title: Place words: on, under, inside, in front
guide.text:
Words for position follow the noun in its possessive form, as if you were saying 'at the table's top'.

উপরে (upore) on, above - in Kolkata speech usually ওপরে (opore)
নিচে (niche) under, below
ভেতরে (bhetore) inside - written form ভিতরে
বাইরে (baaire) outside
সামনে (shaamne) in front of
পেছনে (pechhone) behind - written form পিছনে
পাশে (paashe) beside
মধ্যে (moddhe) in the middle of, among, within

So: টেবিলের উপরে, 'on the table'; খাটের নিচে, 'under the bed'; বাড়ির সামনে, 'in front of the house'; দোকানের পাশে, 'next to the shop'.

examples.english: The book is on top of the table.
The cat is under the bed.

phrases.note: The person takes -ke; the thing takes no ending.

phrases.english: I am going to the market.

phrases.note: -te after a vowel other than aa.
Rice meals are traditionally eaten with the right hand.

phrases.english: I cut fruit with a knife.
I am going with a friend.
phrases.note: In Bangladesh: বন্ধুর সাথে (bondhur shaathe).

phrases.english: The book is on top of the table.
The shop is near the station.
The cat is under the bed.
phrases.note: The written form of 'cat' is বিড়াল (biraal).

units.title: Asking questions
units.description: Ask what, who, where, when, why, how and how much, and turn any statement into a yes/no question.

guide.title: Question words stay in place
guide.text:
English moves the question word to the front. Bengali leaves it where the answer would go, which is normally just before the verb.

আপনি কোথায় যাচ্ছেন? - 'you where are-going?' The answer drops into the same slot: আমি বাজারে যাচ্ছি।

The main question words:
কী (kee) what
কে (ke) who - কার (kaar) whose - কাকে (kaake) whom, to whom
কোথায় (kothaay) where
কখন (kokhon) when, at what time - কবে (kobe) when, on what day
কেন (keno) why
কেমন (kemon) how, what like
কোন (kon) which
কত (koto) how much
কী করে (kee kore) or কীভাবে (keebhaabe) how, in what way

Most of them begin with ক, just as English ones begin with wh-. In কেন and কেমন the e is the a of 'cat'.

guide.title: Yes/no questions: কি with a short i
guide.text:
To ask a yes/no question, you can simply say the statement with a rising tone: আপনি বাঙালি? 'You are Bengali?'

Or you can add the little word কি (ki), usually right after the subject: আপনি কি বাঙালি? It has no meaning of its own; it only announces that a yes/no question is coming, like 'do' or 'is' at the start of an English question.

This কি is spelt with the SHORT vowel sign. The word for 'what', কী, is spelt with the LONG one. They sound almost the same (কী carries the stress), but in writing the difference matters:

আপনি কি খাবেন? - Will you eat? (yes or no)
আপনি কী খাবেন? - What will you eat?

To answer, repeat the verb: খাব (I will) or খাব না (I won't).

guide.title: How much and how many
guide.text:
কত (koto) asks for an amount or a number: কত টাকা? 'how much money?'; কত দূর? 'how far?'. It is also the word for asking any number - a price, a phone number, a date, someone's age: আপনার বয়স কত? 'what is your age?'

For counting things, add the classifier: কটা (kotaa) 'how many (things)', কজন (kojon) 'how many (people)'. These are often written ক'টা and ক'জন, or in full কয়টা, কয়জন.

কটা is also how you ask the time: কটা বাজে?

guide.title: Checking: তো and না
guide.text:
Two small words turn a statement into 'isn't it?' or 'won't you?'.

তো (to) at the end of a sentence expects the answer yes: আপনি চা খাবেন তো? 'You'll have tea, won't you?'; ভালো তো? 'All well, I hope?'

তাই না? (taai naa), literally 'so, no?', is the general tag 'isn't that so?'.

না (naa) alone at the end also works as a tag: খুব গরম, না? 'Very hot, isn't it?'

phrases.note: কী with the long vowel sign means 'what'.
কখন asks for a time of day; কবে (kobe) asks for a day or date.
টাকা is the rupee in India and the taka in Bangladesh, and also simply 'money'.
কী করে, 'doing what', is the everyday 'how'.
কি with the short vowel sign only marks a yes/no question.
Familiar form.
Bengali 'eats' tea, water and all other drinks.

units.title: Saying no: naa, noy, nei, -ni
units.description: Make any sentence negative, choosing correctly between the four negatives of Bengali.

guide.title: না after the verb
guide.text:
For most verbs, the negative is made by putting না (naa) AFTER the verb, at the very end of the sentence. This is the opposite of Hindi and of English.

আমি যাব - I will go. আমি যাব না - I will not go.
আমি মাছ খাই - I eat fish. আমি মাছ খাই না - I don't eat fish.
আমি বুঝতে পারছি - I understand. আমি বুঝতে পারছি না - I don't understand.

This works for the simple present, the continuous tenses, the future and the simple past.

guide.title: 'Is not': নই, নও, নয়, নন
guide.text:
A sentence with no verb - 'A is B' - has a special negative verb, which takes the personal endings:

আমি ... নই (noi) - I am not
তুমি ... নও (nou, said no-o) - you are not (familiar)
তুই ... নস (nosh) - you are not (intimate)
সে / এটা ... নয় (noy) - he/she/it is not
আপনি / তিনি ... নন (non) - you are not (polite), he/she is not (respected)

আমি ডাক্তার - I am a doctor. আমি ডাক্তার নই - I am not a doctor.
এটা আমার - This is mine. এটা আমার নয় - This is not mine.

In casual speech many people just say না here (এটা আমার না), but নয় is the standard form and always correct.

guide.title: 'Is not there', 'do not have': নেই
guide.text:
The negative of আছে is নেই (nei). You never say আছে না.

নেই does not change for person or respect: আমি নেই, সে নেই, উনি নেই.

It means 'is not present', 'there is no ...' and 'do not have':

ও বাড়িতে নেই - He is not at home.
এখানে কেউ নেই - There is nobody here.
আমার সময় নেই - I have no time.

It also negates states expressed with আছে: আমি ভালো আছি 'I am well' - আমি ভালো নেই 'I am not well'.

So: এটা চা নয় (This is not tea - it is something else) but চা নেই (There is no tea).

guide.title: 'Did not', 'have not': -নি
guide.text:
The completed tenses - 'I have eaten', 'I had gone' - do not take না. Their negative is made from the SIMPLE PRESENT form of the verb with -নি (-ni) attached:

আমি খেয়েছি - I have eaten. আমি খাইনি - I haven't eaten / I didn't eat.
সে এসেছে - He has come. সে আসেনি - He hasn't come / He didn't come.
আমি বলেছিলাম - I had said. আমি বলিনি - I didn't say.

So the pattern is: খাই + নি, আসে + নি, যায় + নি, করেন + নি. The verb keeps the ending that matches its subject.

এখনো ... -নি is 'not yet', and কখনো ... -নি is 'never'.

The negative of ছিল ('was') is ছিল না: কেউ ছিল না, 'nobody was there'.

guide.title: 'Don't!'
guide.text:
A negative command is made with না after the verb, but the verb is in a future-type form rather than the plain command form.

Polite (আপনি): the future form + না. যাবেন না - don't go. করবেন না - don't do (it).

Familiar (তুমি): a special form ending in -o, + না. যেয়ো না - don't go. কোরো না - don't do. বোলো না - don't say.

Intimate (তুই): the present form + না. যাস না, করিস না.

The commands themselves are the subject of a later unit; for now, learn the polite pattern -ben naa.

phrases.note: না follows the verb.
নও is two short syllables: no-o.
নন is the respectful form, matching উনি.
The negative of ভালো আছি.
Present form খাই + নি, not খেয়েছি না.
কিছু with a negative means 'nothing'.

phrases.english: I have never been to Delhi.

phrases.note: Polite form: চিন্তা করবেন না (chintaa korben naa).

units.title: This, that, here, there
units.description: Point to things near and far, and use the matching words for here, there, now, then, this way and so much.

guide.title: Three pointers: e-, o-, she-
guide.text:
Bengali has three pointing roots, and a whole family of words is built on each.

এ- (e-) is 'this': near the speaker.
ও- (o-) is 'that': away from the speaker but in sight, something you can point at.
সে- (she-) is 'that': the one already mentioned, usually not in sight.

Before a noun they appear as এই (ei), ওই (oi) and সেই (shei), and the noun normally takes the definite ending -টা: এই বইটা 'this book', ওই বাড়িটা 'that house', সেই লোকটা 'that man (we were talking about)'.

Standing alone, for a thing, they are এটা (etaa), ওটা (otaa), সেটা (shetaa): 'this one', 'that one', 'that / it'.

For several things: এগুলো (egulo) 'these', ওগুলো (ogulo) 'those', সেগুলো (shegulo).

guide.title: Here, there, this way, that way
guide.text:
The same three roots give the place words:

এখানে (ekhaane) here - ওখানে (okhaane) there (in sight) - সেখানে (shekhaane) there (the place mentioned)
এদিকে (edike) this way, over here - ওদিকে (odike) that way, over there

'From here' is এখান থেকে (ekhaan theke), without the final -e: the ending -e is the 'at' ending and থেকে replaces it.

The question words belong to the same pattern with ক-: কোথায় (where), কোনদিকে (which way).

examples.english: How far is it from here?

guide.title: Now, then, like this, so much
guide.text:
More members of the family:

Time: এখন (ekhon) now - তখন (tokhon) then - কখন when?
Manner: এরকম (erokom) or এমন (emon) like this, such - ওরকম (orokom) like that - কেমন how?
Amount: এত (eto) this much, so much - অত (oto) or তত (toto) that much - কত how much?

এত is very common as an exclamation: এত দাম! 'so expensive!'; এত লোক! 'so many people!'

In এখন, এত and এমন the first vowel is the a of 'cat'.

examples.english: Give me another one like this.

phrases.note: After এই the noun normally takes -taa.
সেটা refers back to what was just said.
সেই: the man both speakers already know about.
The e of এত is the a of 'cat', and the final o is said.

phrases.english: Give me another one like this.

units.title: Counting and 'the': -taa, -ti, -jon, -khaanaa
units.description: Use the classifier endings to say 'the', to count things and people, and to talk about a little or a lot.

guide.title: -টা: 'the', and the counting ending
guide.text:
The ending -টা (-taa) has two jobs.

On a noun it means 'the': বই 'book' - বইটা 'the book'; চাবি 'key' - চাবিটা 'the key'. Use it when both of you know which one is meant.

On a number it lets you count things: একটা বই 'one book, a book', পাঁচটা বই 'five books'. A number cannot normally stand directly before a noun without it. The noun stays singular.

Kolkata speech has three irregular forms: দুটো (duto), তিনটে (tinte), চারটে (chaarte). Everything else is regular: একটা, পাঁচটা, ছটা, সাতটা, আটটা, নটা, দশটা. Bangladesh standard uses -টা throughout: দুইটা, তিনটা, চারটা.

It also attaches to other counting words: কটা (kotaa) 'how many?', কয়েকটা (koyektaa) 'a few', অনেকগুলো 'many'.

guide.title: Number before or after the noun
guide.text:
Where you put the counted number changes the meaning.

Number + classifier BEFORE the noun is indefinite: দুটো বই - 'two books' (any two).

Noun first, then number + classifier, is definite: বই দুটো - 'the two books'.

In the same way একটা বই is 'a book', and বইটা is 'the book'.

guide.title: -টি, -জন, -খানা
guide.text:
-টি (-ti) is a gentler version of -টা. It suggests that the thing is small, dear or being spoken of politely, and it is the normal form in writing: একটি ছেলে 'a boy', ছেলেটি 'the boy', মেয়েটি 'the girl'. In speech -টা about a person can sound offhand; -টি never does.

-জন (-jon) counts people: একজন (ekjon), দুজন (dujon), তিনজন, কজন? It goes on the number only, never on the noun: একজন লোক 'a man', দুজন ছাত্র 'two students'. People can also be counted with -টা or -টি when they are children or when you are being casual: দুটো ছেলে.

-খানা (-khaanaa) is used for solid, flat or made objects - books, letters, saris, plates, houses, rooms: একখানা শাড়ি 'a sari', বইখানা 'the book'. It is optional (-টা is always possible) but you will hear it often in West Bengal. A lighter form is -খানি.

guide.title: Plural, and 'a little'
guide.text:
-গুলো (-gulo) is the plural of -টা: 'the ...s'. বইগুলো 'the books', এগুলো 'these'. The politer and written form is -গুলি (-guli). It is only used when the plural is definite and no number is given; after a number the noun stays bare.

For people, the plural ending is -রা (-raa): ছেলেরা 'the boys', বাচ্চারা 'the children'.

-টুকু (-tuku) means 'the little bit of': জলটুকু 'that little bit of water', এইটুকু 'just this much'.

একটু (ektu) is 'a little' of something you cannot count, and by extension the word that softens every request: একটু চিনি 'a little sugar', একটু দাঁড়ান 'wait a little'. Do not confuse it with একটা, 'one (thing)'.

examples.english: Put the books on the table.
Drink up that little bit of water.

phrases.note: For family members the verb আছে is often left out.
In Bangladesh: তিনটা (tintaa).
In Bangladesh: চারটা (chaartaa).
Number after the noun = definite.
-ti is the polite, affectionate form of -taa.
The respectful verb ending is used for an adult stranger.
-khaanaa suits flat, made objects.

phrases.english: Put the books on the table.

phrases.note: একটু for things you cannot count.

phrases.english: Drink up that little bit of water.

units.title: Describing things
units.description: Describe people and things, say 'very' and 'a bit', and compare: bigger than, the best.

guide.title: Adjectives never change
guide.text:
A Bengali adjective has one form only. It does not change for gender, for number or for case: বড় ঘর 'a big room', বড় ঘরগুলো 'the big rooms', বড় মেয়ে 'the elder daughter'.

Before a noun it works as in English: একটা লাল শাড়ি, 'a red sari'. The order is number - adjective - noun.

To say that something IS big, put the adjective after the noun, with no verb: ঘরটা বড়, 'the room (is) big'. The negative uses নয়: ঘরটা বড় নয়.

Some useful pairs: বড় boro big / ছোট chhoto small; ভালো bhaalo good / খারাপ khaaraap bad; নতুন notun new / পুরোনো purono old (of things); গরম gorom hot / ঠান্ডা thaandaa cold; সহজ shohoj easy / কঠিন kothin hard; সস্তা shostaa cheap / দামি daami expensive; লম্বা lombaa long, tall / বেঁটে bente short (of a person).

guide.title: Very, quite, a bit, too
guide.text:
Words of degree go before the adjective.

খুব (khub) very
বেশ (besh) quite, pretty
একটু (ektu) a bit
বেশি (beshi) too, too much - before an adjective (বেশি গরম, 'too hot') or after the thing there is too much of: ঝাল বেশি, 'too spicy'
একদম (ekdom) absolutely
দারুণ (daarun) terrific - used on its own as praise

There is no special word for 'too' as in 'too hot'; খুব গরম or বড্ড গরম (boddo gorom) covers it, or বেশি গরম.

examples.english: The food is a bit spicy.

guide.title: Bigger than, the biggest
guide.text:
Adjectives have no -er or -est forms. To compare, the thing compared WITH takes the possessive ending and is followed by চেয়ে (cheye) 'than'. The adjective is unchanged.

ও আমার চেয়ে বড় - 'he my than big' - He is older (bigger) than me.
এটা ওটার চেয়ে ভালো - This is better than that.

থেকে (theke), 'from', is used in exactly the same way and is very common in speech: আমার থেকে বড়.

You can add আরও (aaro) 'more' or বেশি for emphasis: আরও বড়, 'even bigger'.

The superlative is সবচেয়ে (shobcheye), 'than all': সবচেয়ে ভালো 'the best', সবচেয়ে সস্তা 'the cheapest'.

'Like' is মতো (moto) after a possessive: আমার মতো, 'like me'.

guide.title: Colours
guide.text:
The basic colour words: লাল (laal) red; নীল (neel) blue; সবুজ (shobuj) green; হলুদ (holud) yellow - also the word for turmeric; সাদা (shaadaa) white; কালো (kaalo) black; বাদামি (baadaami) brown; গোলাপি (golaapi) pink; কমলা (komlaa) orange.

'What colour?' is কী রং? (kee rong). 'Colour' itself is রং.

phrases.english: This one is big, that one is small.
phrases.note: Both adjectives keep their final o.
Order: number, adjective, noun.

phrases.english: The food is a bit spicy.
phrases.note: ঝাল is chilli-hot; গরম is hot to the touch.
মিষ্টি is both 'sweet' (adjective) and 'a sweet'.
Of people, বড় and ছোট mean older and younger.

units.title: Present: what you usually do
units.description: Talk about habits and facts in the simple present, with the right ending for every person, for ten essential verbs.

guide.title: Stem + five endings
guide.text:
A dictionary gives a Bengali verb as a verbal noun ending in -আ or -ওয়া: করা (koraa) 'to do, doing', বলা (bolaa) 'to say', খাওয়া (khaaowaa) 'to eat'. Take off that ending and you have the stem: কর-, বল-, খা-.

The simple present adds one of five endings to the stem:

আমি / আমরা: -ই (-i)
তুমি / তোমরা: -ও (-o)
তুই / তোরা: -ইস (-ish)
সে / ও / তারা: -এ (-e)
আপনি / তিনি / উনি: -এন (-en)

There is no separate plural form, and no difference between he and she.

This tense is used for habits (I walk every morning), for general facts (the shop opens at ten), and for what you know, think, want or like.

guide.title: The stem vowel shifts
guide.text:
In many verbs the vowel of the stem is 'higher' before the endings -i and -ish, and 'lower' before -o, -e and -en. In some verbs the spelling shows the change, in others only the pronunciation does.

Spelling changes (i / e and u / o):
লেখা to write: আমি লিখি (likhi) - সে লেখে (lekhe) - আপনি লেখেন (lekhen)
শোনা to hear: আমি শুনি (shuni) - সে শোনে (shone) - আপনি শোনেন (shonen)
কেনা to buy: আমি কিনি (kini) - সে কেনে (kene)
বোঝা to understand: আমি বুঝি (bujhi) - সে বোঝে (bojhe)

Sound changes only:
করা, বলা: in করি, বলি the first vowel is the closed o; in করো, করে, করেন it is the open o of 'hot'.
দেখা to see: দেখি (dekhi) has a true e; দেখো, দেখে, দেখেন have the a of 'cat'.

Verbs whose stem has আ never change: থাকা - থাকি, থাকো, থাকে; জানা - জানি, জানে.

guide.title: Stems ending in a vowel: eat, go
guide.text:
When the stem ends in আ, the endings shorten: -e becomes -য় (-y) and -en becomes -ন (-n).

খাওয়া to eat (also to drink, to smoke): আমি খাই (khaai), তুমি খাও (khaao), তুই খাস (khaash), সে খায় (khaay), আপনি খান (khaan).

যাওয়া to go: আমি যাই (jaai), তুমি যাও (jaao), তুই যাস (jaash), সে যায় (jaay), আপনি যান (jaan).

In the same way: পাওয়া to get - পাই, পাও, পাস, পায়, পান; চাওয়া to want - চাই, চাও, চাস, চায়, চান.

guide.title: Give, take, be
guide.text:
Three very common verbs have a stem that switches between i, e and a/o.

দেওয়া to give: আমি দিই (dii), তুমি দাও (daao), তুই দিস (dish), সে দেয় (dey), আপনি দেন (den).

নেওয়া to take: আমি নিই (nii), তুমি নাও (naao), তুই নিস (nish), সে নেয় (ney), আপনি নেন (nen).

হওয়া to be, become, happen: আমি হই (hoi), তুমি হও (hou, said ho-o), তুই হস (hosh), সে হয় (hoy), আপনি হন (hon).

In দেয়, দেন, নেয়, নেন the e is the a of 'cat'.

হয় is not the everyday 'is' (that is the zero verb or আছে). It means 'happens, becomes, is as a rule': এখানে খুব বৃষ্টি হয়, 'it rains a lot here'.

guide.title: Come, stay, see, say
guide.text:
The remaining verbs of the essential ten are regular.

আসা to come: আসি (aashi), আসো (aasho), আসিস (aashish), আসে (aashe), আসেন (aashen).

থাকা to stay, live: থাকি (thaaki), থাকো (thaako), থাকিস (thaakish), থাকে (thaake), থাকেন (thaaken).

দেখা to see: দেখি (dekhi), দেখো (dekho), দেখিস (dekhish), দেখে (dekhe), দেখেন (dekhen).

বলা to say, speak: বলি (boli), বলো (bolo), বলিস (bolish), বলে (bole), বলেন (bolen).

Many everyday verbs are a noun + করা: কাজ করা 'to work', রান্না করা 'to cook', ফোন করা 'to phone'. Only করা changes.

phrases.note: The respectful -en for one's father.
The same ending as for 'I'.
Drinks are 'eaten' in Bengali.
The stem vowel is o before -e, u before -i: আমি শুনি (aami shuni).

phrases.english: They play football in the afternoon.

phrases.note: The stem vowel is i before -i, e before -e: সে লেখে (she lekhe).

units.title: Happening now
units.description: Say what is going on at this moment, what is about to happen and what was going on, with the -chh- forms.

guide.title: Stem + ছ + ending
guide.text:
The present continuous - 'I am doing' - is made by adding -ছ- (-chh-) and the personal ending to the stem. The stem takes its 'high' vowel (the one used before -i).

করা to do:
আমি করছি (korchhi) I am doing
তুমি করছ (korchho) you are doing, familiar
তুই করছিস (korchhish) you are doing, intimate
সে করছে (korchhe) he/she is doing
আপনি / তিনি করছেন (korchhen) you are doing (polite), he/she is doing (respected)

The তুমি form is spelt without a vowel sign but ends in o: করছ = korchho.

In the same way: বলছি (bolchhi) I am saying; দেখছি (dekhchhi) I am looking; আসছি (aashchhi) I am coming; থাকছি (thaakchhi) I am staying; লিখছি (likhchhi) I am writing; শুনছি (shunchhi) I am listening.

The negative just adds না: আমি করছি না।

guide.title: After a vowel: -চ্ছ-
guide.text:
When the stem ends in a vowel, the sign is doubled to -চ্ছ- (-chchh-).

খাওয়া: খাচ্ছি (khaachchhi), খাচ্ছ (khaachchho), খাচ্ছিস, খাচ্ছে, খাচ্ছেন
যাওয়া: যাচ্ছি (jaachchhi), যাচ্ছ, যাচ্ছিস, যাচ্ছে, যাচ্ছেন
দেওয়া: দিচ্ছি (dichchhi), দিচ্ছ, দিচ্ছিস, দিচ্ছে, দিচ্ছেন
নেওয়া: নিচ্ছি (nichchhi), নিচ্ছ, নিচ্ছিস, নিচ্ছে, নিচ্ছেন
হওয়া: হচ্ছি (hochchhi), হচ্ছ, হচ্ছিস, হচ্ছে, হচ্ছেন

হচ্ছে, 'is happening', is how Bengali reports weather and events: বৃষ্টি হচ্ছে 'it is raining', কী হচ্ছে? 'what is going on?'

guide.title: Now, and very soon
guide.text:
The continuous is used for what is in progress at this moment, as in English.

It is also used for the immediate future, especially with verbs of movement. আমি আসছি, 'I am coming', is what you say as you LEAVE a room or a shop for a moment: 'I'll be right back'. কাল আমি দিল্লি যাচ্ছি is 'I am going to Delhi tomorrow'.

Unlike English, Bengali is happy to use the continuous with verbs of feeling and understanding: আমি বুঝতে পারছি না, 'I am not able to understand'; ভালো লাগছে, 'it is feeling good'.

For a state that began in the past and still continues, Bengali uses a present tense where English says 'have been': আমি দু বছর এখানে আছি - 'I have been here for two years'.

examples.english: I'm coming. / I'll be right back.

guide.title: Was doing
guide.text:
For the past continuous, put -ছিল- (-chhil-) in place of -ছ- and use the past set of endings (-aam, -e, -i, -o, -en):

আমি করছিলাম (korchhilaam) I was doing
তুমি করছিলে (korchhile)
তুই করছিলি (korchhili)
সে করছিল (korchhilo)
আপনি / তিনি করছিলেন (korchhilen)

After a vowel: খাচ্ছিলাম (khaachchhilaam) I was eating; যাচ্ছিলাম (jaachchhilaam) I was going.

phrases.note: 'Eating rice' is the ordinary way to say having lunch or dinner.

phrases.english: I'm coming. / I'll be right back.
phrases.note: Said when stepping out for a moment, and also as a goodbye.
Kolkata form. In Bangladesh: ঘুমাচ্ছে (ghumaachchhe).

units.title: The past
units.description: Talk about what has happened, what happened at a definite time, how things were and what you used to do.

guide.title: Have done: -echh-
guide.text:
The tense you need most is the present perfect. It is used for anything that has happened and still matters now - which covers most of what English says with a simple past in conversation: 'I ate', 'he left', 'did you see it?'

It is built on the -e form of the verb (করে, বলে, দেখে) + ছ + the present endings:

আমি করেছি (korechhi) I have done / I did
তুমি করেছ (korechho)
তুই করেছিস (korechhish)
সে করেছে (korechhe)
আপনি / তিনি করেছেন (korechhen)

The essential verbs:
বলা - বলেছি (bolechhi); দেখা - দেখেছি (dekhechhi); থাকা - থেকেছি (thekechhi)
খাওয়া - খেয়েছি (kheyechhi); দেওয়া - দিয়েছি (diyechhi); নেওয়া - নিয়েছি (niyechhi); হওয়া - হয়েছি (hoyechhi)
আসা - এসেছি (eshechhi)
যাওয়া - গিয়েছি (giyechhi), in Kolkata speech almost always shortened to গেছি (gechhi): গেছ, গেছিস, গেছে, গেছেন.

Its negative is the present form + নি: করিনি, যায়নি (see the unit on negation).

guide.title: Did: the simple past in -l-
guide.text:
The simple past adds -ল- (-l-) and the past endings to the stem:

আমি করলাম (korlaam) I did
তুমি করলে (korle)
তুই করলি (korli)
সে করল (korlo)
আপনি / তিনি করলেন (korlen)

It is used for something that happened just now or a moment ago, and for telling a story step by step: 'I went in, I saw him, he said ...'. For a single past fact in conversation the perfect (above) is more usual.

The essential verbs:
বলা - বললাম (bollaam), বলল (bollo); দেখা - দেখলাম (dekhlaam); থাকা - থাকলাম (thaaklaam)
খাওয়া - খেলাম (khelaam), খেল (khelo); দেওয়া - দিলাম (dilaam), দিল (dilo); নেওয়া - নিলাম (nilaam), নিল (nilo)
হওয়া - হলাম (holaam), হলো (holo)
আসা - এলাম (elaam), এলে, এলি, এল (elo), এলেন (elen)
যাওয়া - গেলাম (gelaam), গেলে, গেলি, গেল (gelo), গেলেন (gelen)

In West Bengal you will also hear the first person with -লুম: করলুম, গেলুম.

guide.title: Did, back then: -echhil-
guide.text:
When the event belongs to a finished time in the past - yesterday, last year, in childhood - Bengali uses the past perfect, where English still says 'went', 'came', 'saw'.

It is the -e form + ছিল + the past endings:

আমি করেছিলাম (korechhilaam)
তুমি করেছিলে (korechhile)
তুই করেছিলি (korechhili)
সে করেছিল (korechhilo)
আপনি / তিনি করেছিলেন (korechhilen)

যাওয়া - গিয়েছিলাম (giyechhilaam); আসা - এসেছিলাম (eshechhilaam); খাওয়া - খেয়েছিলাম (kheyechhilaam); দেওয়া - দিয়েছিলাম (diyechhilaam).

A rule of thumb: with a past time word (কাল, গত বছর), use this tense.

examples.english: We went to Darjeeling last year.

guide.title: Was, and used to
guide.text:
The past of both the zero verb and আছে is ছিল-:

আমি ছিলাম (chhilaam) I was
তুমি ছিলে (chhile)
তুই ছিলি (chhili)
সে ছিল (chhilo)
আপনি / তিনি ছিলেন (chhilen)

So: আজ গরম (today is hot) - কাল গরম ছিল (yesterday was hot); আমার একটা গাড়ি আছে (I have a car) - আমার একটা গাড়ি ছিল (I had a car). The negative is ছিল না.

'Used to do' is the habitual past: stem + -ত- (-t-) + the past endings (except that তুই takes -ish):

আমি করতাম (kortaam) I used to do
তুমি করতে (korte)
তুই করতিস (kortish)
সে করত (korto)
আপনি / তিনি করতেন (korten)

খাওয়া - খেতাম (khetaam); যাওয়া - যেতাম (jetaam); থাকা - থাকতাম (thaaktaam); আসা - আসতাম (aashtaam).

examples.english: We used to live in Kolkata.

phrases.note: A common friendly question, almost a greeting.
English 'came', but the perfect in Bengali: the day is not over.
গেছে is the everyday short form of গিয়েছে (giyechhe).
The negative of বলেছি.
Simple past: just now, or as part of a story.
The past stem of আসা (to come) is এ-.
Also 'What's the matter?'

phrases.english: We went to Darjeeling last year.
phrases.note: A finished past time calls for the -echhil- tense.
কাল is 'yesterday' here because the verb is past.
Smoking, too, is 'eating' in Bengali.

units.title: The future
units.description: Say what you will do, make plans and offers, and use the time words for tomorrow, later and next week.

guide.title: Stem + ব + ending
guide.text:
The future adds -ব- (-b-) and its own endings to the stem:

আমি করব (korbo) I will do
তুমি করবে (korbe) you will do, familiar
তুই করবি (korbi) you will do, intimate
সে করবে (korbe) he/she will do
আপনি / তিনি করবেন (korben) you will do (polite), he/she will do (respected)

Note that তুমি and সে share a form in the future. The first person is spelt করব, without a vowel sign, but ends in o: korbo. (You will also see করবো.)

The stem takes its 'high' vowel: লেখা - লিখব (likhbo); শোনা - শুনব (shunbo); কেনা - কিনব (kinbo).

Regular verbs: বলা - বলব (bolbo); দেখা - দেখব (dekhbo); আসা - আসব (aashbo); থাকা - থাকব (thaakbo).

The negative adds না: আমি করব না।

guide.title: Eat, go, give, take, be
guide.text:
The vowel stems:

খাওয়া: খাব (khaabo), খাবে, খাবি, খাবে, খাবেন
যাওয়া: যাব (jaabo), যাবে, যাবি, যাবে, যাবেন
দেওয়া: দেব (debo), দেবে, দিবি, দেবে, দেবেন
নেওয়া: নেব (nebo), নেবে, নিবি, নেবে, নেবেন
হওয়া: হব (hobo), হবে, হবি, হবে, হবেন

In দেওয়া and নেওয়া the তুই form goes back to i: দিবি, নিবি.

হবে, 'will be, will happen', is extremely common: কাল বৃষ্টি হবে 'it will rain tomorrow'; কী হবে? 'what will happen?'; হবে না 'it won't work, it won't do'; দেখা হবে 'we'll meet'. Since the zero verb has no future, হবে also supplies 'will be': ভালো হবে, 'it will be good'. For 'will be (somewhere)' use থাকা, 'to stay': আমি বাড়িতে থাকব।

examples.english: We will go the day after tomorrow.

guide.title: What the future is used for
guide.text:
Besides plain future time, this tense has three everyday uses.

Intention: 'I want to go to the airport' is simply আমি এয়ারপোর্টে যাব, 'I will go'. To a shopkeeper, আমি এটা নেব - 'I'll take this'.

Offers and polite questions: চা খাবেন? 'Will you have tea?'; আপনি কী খাবেন? 'What will you have?'; একটু সরবেন? 'Would you move over a little?'

Asking what to do, in the first person: কী করব? 'What shall I do?'; কোথায় রাখব? 'Where shall I put it?'

Remember that the continuous is also used for a fixed plan with a verb of movement: কাল যাচ্ছি।

guide.title: Time words
guide.text:
আজ (aaj) today
কাল (kaal) tomorrow - and also yesterday; the verb tense tells which. To be explicit: আগামীকাল (aagaameekaal) tomorrow, গতকাল (gotokaal) yesterday.
পরশু (porshu) the day after tomorrow - and also the day before yesterday
এখন (ekhon) now; এক্ষুনি (ekkhuni) right now, this minute
পরে (pore) later; আগে (aage) before, earlier
আগামী (aagaamee) next, coming: আগামী সপ্তাহে (aagaamee shoptaahe) next week
গত (goto) last: গত মাসে (goto maashe) last month
সামনের (shaamner) and পরের (porer) are the everyday words for 'next': সামনের সপ্তাহে।

phrases.note: 'kaal' means both tomorrow and yesterday; the verb tense tells which.

phrases.english: We will go the day after tomorrow.
I will give you the money.

phrases.note: Also 'I'll look into it'.

units.title: Requests and commands
units.description: Ask people to do things at each level of respect, tell them not to, and say 'let's go'.

guide.title: Three command forms
guide.text:
Each level of 'you' has its own command form.

আপনি: stem + -উন (-un). করুন (korun) 'please do'. For vowel stems, just -ন: খান (khaan), যান (jaan).

তুমি: stem + -ও (-o). করো (koro) 'do'. Vowel stems: খাও (khaao), যাও (jaao).

তুই: the bare stem. কর (kor) 'do'. Vowel stems: খা (khaa), যা (jaa).

The আপনি form is polite in itself; no word for 'please' is needed. The stem takes its 'high' vowel before -un: লিখুন (likhun) write, শুনুন (shunun) listen, দেখুন (dekhun) look, বলুন (bolun) say.

guide.title: The commands you need
guide.text:
Polite - familiar - intimate:

করা do: করুন - করো - কর
বলা say: বলুন - বলো - বল
দেখা look: দেখুন - দেখো - দেখ
থাকা stay: থাকুন (thaakun) - থাকো (thaako) - থাক (thaak)
বসা sit: বসুন (boshun) - বসো (bosho) - বস (bosh)
খাওয়া eat: খান - খাও - খা
যাওয়া go: যান - যাও - যা
আসা come: আসুন (aashun) - এসো (esho) - আয় (aay)
দেওয়া give: দিন (din) - দাও (daao) - দে (de)
নেওয়া take: নিন (nin) - নাও (naao) - নে (ne)

আসা is irregular in the familiar and intimate forms: এসো, আয়.

guide.title: Softer, and for later
guide.text:
একটু (ektu), 'a little', before the verb takes the edge off any command: একটু দাঁড়ান, 'wait a moment'; একটু সরুন, 'move over a little'.

The future form is used as a command for something to be done later, or as a courteous request and good wish: কাল আসবেন, 'come tomorrow'; ভালো থাকবেন, 'keep well'; আবার আসবেন, 'do come again'.

তুমি has its own 'later' command ending in -o with a changed stem vowel: কোরো (koro), বোলো (bolo), এসো (esho), যেয়ো (jeyo), দিয়ো (diyo): কাল এসো, 'come tomorrow'.

guide.title: Don't
guide.text:
Negative commands use the 'later' forms + না:

আপনি: future + না. করবেন না (korben naa), যাবেন না, রাখবেন না.
তুমি: কোরো না (koro naa), যেয়ো না (jeyo naa), বোলো না (bolo naa), দিয়ো না (diyo naa).
তুই: present form + না. করিস না (korish naa), যাস না (jaash naa), ধরিস না (dhorish naa).

guide.title: Let's, let me, shall I?
guide.text:
চলা (cholaa) 'to move' gives 'come on, let's go': চলুন (cholun), চলো (cholo), চল (chol). It is usually followed by a first-person present verb: চলুন, যাই - 'come, let's go'; চলো, খাই - 'come on, let's eat'.

The first-person present on its own, said as a question, asks permission: আমি যাই? 'Shall I go? May I go?'; আসি? 'May I come in?' or 'May I leave now?'; দেখি 'let me see'.

'Let me do' is আমাকে + the -te form of the verb + দিন: আমাকে যেতে দিন, 'let me go'; আমাকে বলতে দিন, 'let me speak'.

phrases.note: আয় is the irregular তুই command of আসা.
দাঁড়ানো is 'to stand' and also 'to wait'.
A warm way to end a conversation or a letter.
Blunt. The polite version is একটু চুপ করুন (ektu chup korun).

units.title: Want, need, can, must
units.description: Say what you want, need, can do, may do, have to do and ought to do.

guide.title: The -te form of the verb
guide.text:
'To do' after another verb - want to go, can read, have to wait - is the infinitive, made with -তে (-te) on the 'high' stem:

করা - করতে (korte) to do
বলা - বলতে (bolte); দেখা - দেখতে (dekhte); আসা - আসতে (aashte); থাকা - থাকতে (thaakte)
লেখা - লিখতে (likhte); শোনা - শুনতে (shunte); বোঝা - বুঝতে (bujhte); পড়া - পড়তে (porte)
খাওয়া - খেতে (khete); যাওয়া - যেতে (jete); পাওয়া - পেতে (pete)
দেওয়া - দিতে (dite); নেওয়া - নিতে (nite); হওয়া - হতে (hote)

It always comes BEFORE the verb it depends on: যেতে চাই, 'to-go I-want'.

guide.title: Want: চাওয়া
guide.text:
চাওয়া (chaaowaa) 'to want' is a regular vowel-stem verb: আমি চাই (chaai), তুমি চাও (chaao), তুই চাস (chaash), সে চায় (chaay), আপনি চান (chaan).

Want to do something: the -te form + চাই. আমি বাড়ি যেতে চাই, 'I want to go home'.

Want a thing: আমি এটা চাই is possible, but it can sound demanding. The idiomatic way to say 'I need / I'd like' is the possessive + thing + চাই, where চাই does not change: আমার এটা চাই, 'I want this'; আপনার কী চাই? 'What would you like?'

Politely declining: চাই না, or better লাগবে না, 'it won't be needed'.

examples.english: I don't want to eat anything.

guide.title: Need: লাগবে and দরকার
guide.text:
Bengali has no verb 'to need' with a person as subject. The person who needs is put in the possessive, and the thing needed is the subject.

লাগা (laagaa) 'to be required': আমার একটা ঘর লাগবে, 'my one room will-be-required' - I need a room. In the present: কত সময় লাগে? 'how much time does it take?'

দরকার (dorkaar) 'need, necessity': আমার সাহায্য দরকার, 'my help need' - I need help. Negative: দরকার নেই, 'there is no need'.

Both stay the same whoever needs: আপনার কী লাগবে? 'What do you need?'

guide.title: Can and may: পারা
guide.text:
পারা (paaraa) 'to be able' follows the -te form and takes the normal endings: আমি পারি (paari), তুমি পারো (paaro), তুই পারিস (paarish), সে পারে (paare), আপনি পারেন (paaren).

Ability: আমি বাংলা পড়তে পারি, 'I can read Bengali'.
Permission: আমি কি ভেতরে আসতে পারি? 'May I come in?'
Possibility: বৃষ্টি হতে পারে, 'it may rain'.

For being able at this moment, use the continuous: আমি বুঝতে পারছি না, 'I can't understand (what you are saying)'. Past: পারলাম না, 'I couldn't'; future: পারব, 'I'll be able to'.

'Can one ...?' / 'Is it possible to ...?' with no particular subject uses the verbal noun + যাওয়া: এখানে ছবি তোলা যাবে? 'Can photos be taken here?'; যাওয়া যায়, 'one can go'; শোনা যাচ্ছে না, 'it can't be heard'.

examples.english: Is it all right to take photos here?

guide.title: Must and should
guide.text:
'Have to' is the -te form + হবে (hobe), and the person who has to is marked with -কে (or, equally common, the possessive): আমাকে যেতে হবে, 'me-to to-go will-be' - I have to go. হবে does not change with the person.

Present habit: আমাকে রোজ যেতে হয়, 'I have to go every day'. Past: যেতে হলো / যেতে হয়েছিল, 'had to go'. Negative: যেতে হবে না, 'don't have to go'.

'Should' is the verbal noun + উচিত (uchit) 'proper', with the person in the possessive: আপনার যাওয়া উচিত, 'your going is proper' - you should go. Negative: উচিত নয়.

examples.english: You will have to wait a little.

phrases.note: Direct. A shopkeeper would rather ask আপনার কী চাই? or কী লাগবে?

phrases.english: I don't want to eat anything.

phrases.note: The য-ফলা doubles the j: shaa-haaj-jo.
To swim is literally 'to cut a swim'.

phrases.english: Is it all right to take photos here?
phrases.note: Verbal noun + যাওয়া = 'can be done'.

phrases.english: You will have to wait a little.

phrases.note: In Bengali you 'show' yourself to the doctor.

units.title: Have and have not
units.description: Say what you have, had and do not have - belongings, family, time, and aches and colds.

guide.title: 'Mine there is': possessive + আছে
guide.text:
Bengali has no verb 'to have'. Instead of 'I have a car' you say 'my a car exists': আমার একটা গাড়ি আছে।

The owner is in the possessive (আমার, আপনার, ওর, রাজের). The verb আছে agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner, so it is nearly always আছে: আমার ... আছে, আপনার ... আছে, ওদের ... আছে.

The one exception is when what you 'have' is a person who deserves respect: আমার একজন দাদা আছেন, 'I have an elder brother'.

A question needs only a rising tone or কি: আপনার ছেলেমেয়ে আছে? 'Do you have children?'

guide.title: Have not: নেই
guide.text:
The negative of আছে is নেই (nei), for every person: আমার গাড়ি নেই, 'I don't have a car'; আমার সময় নেই, 'I have no time'.

Never say আছে না.

In the negative the noun usually drops একটা: 'I don't have a car' is simply আমার গাড়ি নেই.

examples.english: I don't have time right now.

guide.title: Have it on you: কাছে
guide.text:
For things you are carrying or have available right now - money, a pen, change, a ticket - Bengali says 'near me': আমার কাছে ... আছে.

আমার কাছে টাকা নেই - I have no money on me.
আমার টাকা নেই - I have no money (I am poor).

আপনার কাছে খুচরো আছে? - Do you have change (on you)?

examples.english: I have no money on me.

guide.title: Had, will have
guide.text:
আছে exists only in the present. Its past is ছিল (chhilo): আমার একটা কুকুর ছিল, 'I had a dog'. Negative: ছিল না.

For the future, থাকা (to stay) steps in: কাল আমার সময় থাকবে, 'I will have time tomorrow'; থাকবে না, 'won't have'.

examples.english: We didn't have a TV then.

guide.title: Having a fever, a cold, hunger
guide.text:
Illnesses and bodily feelings are not 'had' with আছে. They 'happen to', 'strike' or 'catch' you, and you are again in the possessive.

হয়েছে (has happened): আমার জ্বর হয়েছে, 'I have a fever'; সর্দি হয়েছে, 'have a cold in the nose'.
লেগেছে (has struck): আমার ঠান্ডা লেগেছে, 'I have caught a cold'.
ধরেছে (has caught): আমার মাথা ধরেছে, 'I have a headache'.
পেয়েছে (has got): আমার খিদে পেয়েছে, 'I am hungry'; তেষ্টা পেয়েছে, 'am thirsty'; ঘুম পেয়েছে, 'am sleepy'.

phrases.note: ছেলেমেয়ে, 'boys-girls', is the usual word for one's children.
শ before ন is a true s: pros-no.
In Bangladesh: ভাংতি (bhaangti).

phrases.english: I have no money on me.

phrases.note: Called out at a door. The polite ending is used because you do not know who will answer.

phrases.english: We didn't have a TV then.

units.title: Two-verb combinations
units.description: Understand and use the verb pairs Bengali relies on: kore deowaa, kore neowaa, hoye jaaowaa, phele deowaa, niye aashaa.

guide.title: Main verb in -e + a helper
guide.text:
Listen to any Bengali conversation and you will hear verbs in pairs: বসে পড়ুন, ভুলে গেছি, লিখে দিন. The first verb carries the meaning; the second, a 'helper', adds a shade - finality, suddenness, for whose benefit - and carries the tense and the personal ending.

The first verb is in the -e form (the same form that the perfect tense is built on):

করা - করে (kore); বলা - বলে (bole); দেখা - দেখে (dekhe); লেখা - লিখে (likhe); বসা - বসে (boshe); রাখা - রেখে (rekhe)
খাওয়া - খেয়ে (kheye); যাওয়া - গিয়ে (giye); আসা - এসে (eshe); দেওয়া - দিয়ে (diye); নেওয়া - নিয়ে (niye); হওয়া - হয়ে (hoye)

On its own this form means 'having done': খেয়ে আসুন, 'having eaten, come' - come after you have eaten.

The helpers are ordinary verbs - give, take, go, throw, fall, rise - used with their meaning bleached. English does something similar with 'eat UP', 'sit DOWN', 'write it OUT'.

guide.title: দেওয়া and নেওয়া: for you, for me
guide.text:
দেওয়া (to give) as a helper means the action is done for someone else, or directed away from the doer. নেওয়া (to take) means it is done for the doer's own benefit.

এটা লিখে দিন - write this down (and give it to me / for me).
এটা লিখে নিন - write this down (for yourself, so you have it).

দরজাটা খুলে দিন - open the door (for me).
একটু দেখে নিন - have a look (to satisfy yourself).

বলে দেওয়া is 'to tell (someone on my behalf), to let know'; করে দেওয়া 'to do for someone'; বুঝিয়ে দেওয়া 'to explain'; রেখে দেওয়া 'to put away, to keep'; খেয়ে নেওয়া 'to eat up, to have one's meal'.

Adding দিন to a request makes it sound like a favour, which is why it is so common in polite speech.

examples.english: Please write this down for me.

guide.title: যাওয়া and ফেলা: gone and done
guide.text:
যাওয়া (to go) as a helper shows a change of state that is complete, usually something that happens by itself: হয়ে গেছে 'it is done, it has happened'; ভুলে গেছি 'I have forgotten'; চলে যান 'go away'; হারিয়ে গেছে 'it has got lost'; থেমে গেছে 'it has stopped'; ভরে গেছে 'it has filled up'.

ফেলা (to throw, drop) shows that someone has done a thing completely, sometimes rashly or by mistake: খেয়ে ফেলেছি 'I have eaten it all up'; বলে ফেলেছি 'I blurted it out'; হারিয়ে ফেলেছি 'I have (gone and) lost it'; করে ফেলুন 'get it done'.

Compare: ফোনটা হারিয়ে গেছে, 'the phone has got lost' (it happened) and আমি ফোনটা হারিয়ে ফেলেছি, 'I have lost the phone' (I did it).

examples.english: I have eaten it all up.

guide.title: ওঠা, পড়া, রাখা
guide.text:
ওঠা (to rise) adds suddenness, a bursting out: হেসে উঠল 'burst out laughing'; চেঁচিয়ে উঠল 'cried out'; জেগে ওঠা 'to wake up'.

পড়া (to fall) is used with verbs of position and involuntary change: বসে পড়া 'to sit down'; শুয়ে পড়া 'to lie down, go to bed'; ঘুমিয়ে পড়া 'to fall asleep'; এসে পড়া 'to turn up'.

রাখা (to keep) means doing something in advance, to have it ready: বলে রাখা 'to tell beforehand'; কিনে রাখা 'to buy and keep'; টিকিট কেটে রাখব 'I'll get the tickets beforehand'.

guide.title: Bring and take; noun + verb
guide.text:
'To bring' and 'to take (somewhere)' are literally 'having taken, come' and 'having taken, go': নিয়ে আসা (niye aashaa) and নিয়ে যাওয়া (niye jaaowaa). ব্যাগটা নিয়ে আসুন, 'bring the bag'; আমাকে নিয়ে চলুন, 'take me along'. Here both verbs keep their full meaning.

A second, even larger group of everyday verbs is a noun or adjective + করা (do), হওয়া (become), দেওয়া (give) or খাওয়া (eat):

কাজ করা to work; ফোন করা to phone; সাহায্য করা to help; অপেক্ষা করা to wait; পছন্দ করা to like; বন্ধ করা to close; শুরু করা to begin; শেষ করা to finish; পরিষ্কার করা to clean
দেখা হওয়া to meet (by chance); শেষ হওয়া to come to an end; দেরি হওয়া to be late
উত্তর দেওয়া to answer; ধন্যবাদ দেওয়া to thank
সিগারেট খাওয়া to smoke

With করা you do it; with হওয়া it happens: কাজটা শেষ করেছি, 'I have finished the job' - কাজটা শেষ হয়েছে, 'the job is finished'.

examples.english: Please take me to the station.

phrases.note: Warmer and more insistent than plain বসুন.

phrases.english: Please write this down for me.
phrases.note: দিন: done for the speaker.
নিন: done for the listener's own use.

phrases.english: I have eaten it all up.

phrases.note: হয়ে গেছে alone means 'done!' or 'it's over'.
চলে যাওয়া is 'to go away'; চলে আসা is 'to come away, come over'.
Also 'put this away' or, said by a customer, 'keep the change'.

phrases.english: Please take me to the station.

phrases.note: For example, before paying for something.

units.title: Food & drink
units.description: Order food and drink, say what you do and do not eat, ask for more or less, and pay.

guide.title: Eating, drinking and the words for food
guide.text:
One verb, খাওয়া (khaaowaa), covers eating, drinking and smoking: ভাত খাই 'I eat rice', চা খাই 'I drink tea', জল খান 'have some water'.

The core of a Bengali meal: ভাত (bhaat) cooked rice; ডাল (daal) lentils; মাছ (maachh) fish; মাংস (maangsho) meat; তরকারি (torkaari) a vegetable dish or curry; রুটি (ruti) flat bread; ডিম (dim) egg; দই (doi) yogurt; মিষ্টি (mishti) sweets.

Also: জল (jol) water; চা (chaa) tea; দুধ (dudh) milk; চিনি (chini) sugar; নুন (nun) salt.

Tastes: ঝাল (jhaal) chilli-hot; মিষ্টি (mishti) sweet; টক (tok) sour; নোনতা (nontaa) salty; তেতো (teto) bitter.

নিরামিষ (niraamish) is vegetarian food; আমিষ (aamish) is fish, meat and eggs.

Bangladesh: water is পানি (paani), salt is লবণ (lobon), meat is often গোশত (gosht), and breakfast or a snack is নাস্তা (naastaa) where West Bengal says জলখাবার (jolkhaabaar).

guide.title: Asking for things
guide.text:
To order or ask, name the thing and add দিন (din) 'give': এক কাপ চা দিন। The future form দেবেন (deben) is a shade more courteous and is used for instructions about how you want something: ঝাল কম দেবেন, 'put in less chilli'.

Quantities come first: এক কাপ চা (a cup of tea), এক প্লেট ভাত (a plate of rice), দুটো রুটি (two rotis), একটু জল (a little water), আর একটু (a little more).
